subject: The Fed may pause. Canada still can't cut.
bodyMarkdown:
If you are renewing a mortgage this winter, Friday moved the odds, and not the way most people assume. Yesterday I wrote about the AI trade knocking a trillion dollars off chip stocks, but the question at both central banks this morning is hike or hold, and nobody serious is talking about a cut.

## What Warsh would not say

Fed chair Kevin Warsh sat down with IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva in Bangkok on Friday at the IMF and World Bank meetings. He got the obvious question and stepped around it. "I won't prejudge what decision we will make at future meetings," he said, as CNBC reported Friday. Markets read the dodge as a no. CNBC reported that futures gave an October hike a 15 per cent chance Friday morning, down from closer to 27 per cent before he spoke. Goldman Sachs economists wrote that the committee will pause this month, then added, "We continue to expect a second and final hike in December." December is where the hike went. The Fed raised in September, its first increase in three years, to a range of 3.75 to 4 per cent. Prices kept climbing anyway. US inflation hit 3.7 per cent in the year to September, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Wednesday, up from 3.4 per cent in August.

## Canada gave back the whole year

Statistics Canada reported on Friday, October 9 that the economy lost 68,300 jobs in September and unemployment climbed to 6.5 per cent. The damage sat in the public sector, mostly health care, social assistance and education. Add August's 41,700 and Canada has handed back every net job it created in 2026. That is normally a rate cut in waiting. We are not getting one. The Bank of Canada has held its policy rate at 2.25 per cent through seven straight meetings, and prediction markets give a hold on October 28 about 61 per cent, with almost all the rest on a hike. RBC senior economist Claire Fan told The Canadian Press the meeting is live and the door is open to a raise, though she does not expect it. The loonie has already touched 1.4293 against the US dollar, its weakest since April 2025.

## Monday is the real test

Two releases land Monday morning, and they matter more to October 28 than anything said in Bangkok. The Globe and Mail previewed both this week: September CPI from Statistics Canada, and the Bank's **Business Outlook Survey**, a quarterly poll asking Canadian firms what they expect for sales, hiring and prices. August headline inflation ran at 3.0 per cent, while the Bank's **core inflation** measures, which strip out the jumpiest prices to show the underlying trend, averaged about 1.95 per cent. If September comes in near 3 per cent while the labour market keeps bleeding, the Bank is caught between a weak economy and inflation above its 2 per cent target. The next jobs report is November 6, after the decision. Monday is the last clean read anyone gets.

## The takeaway

Price your renewal off a hold rather than a cut, and ask your lender today whether you can lock something now instead of waiting for relief that two central banks just declined to promise. Watch Monday's CPI: a 3 in front of that number ends the cut conversation for the rest of 2026. If you own US assets, the weak loonie has been quietly padding your returns, and a December Fed hike would pad them further. I would not count on Warsh keeping quiet twice.
